key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option reduced minimum-only payers by 23% but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, with nudged cardholders enrolling autopay at only slightly above the minimum.
methodology: Field experiment on credit cards with 6-month follow-up using administrative payment data.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's fear: a nudge that shifts nominal enrollment/payment behavior does not change the underlying financial outcome — critical to whether opt-out enrollment changes real saving or just who is nominally enrolled.
limitations: Credit card debt paydown, not savings enrollment
no data beyond 6 months
not a savings-app setting
relevance_reason: Consumer financial product with liquid dynamics (credit card) showing default/nudge effects on nominal enrollment diverge from effects on the real financial outcome — the exact caution the brief raises about the round-up feature.

key_finding: Overview finds automatic enrollment and default investment options raise short-term participation but can generate longer-term participant disengagement, with plan framing and communication shaping outcomes.
methodology: Narrative literature overview of defined-contribution retirement plan design research. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Synthesizes the employer-plan default literature's known short vs long-run divergence, a useful benchmark for how much the effect might shrink in our consumer setting, though the employer-intermediary mechanism does not transfer directly.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not consumer fintech
narrative overview, not a systematic protocol
no consumer or liquid-savings evidence
relevance_reason: Broad synthesis of the default-effect literature the brief calls the closest analogous body of work, providing baseline effect patterns even though the setting differs.

key_finding: Argues default enrollment raises short-term retirement participation but induces passivity — low contribution rates, non-engagement, and account churn — such that participation alone is an insufficient welfare measure.
methodology: Policy/narrative review article. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States directly the disengagement risk our support team worries about, and proposes mitigations (auto-escalation, re-enrollment reminders) relevant to how we might design the round-up default to avoid vanity enrollment.
limitations: US employer retirement plans, not a consumer product
narrative/policy article, not an empirical study
no effect sizes given
relevance_reason: Explicitly frames the enrollment-vs-passivity trade-off the brief asks about, even though set in the employer-plan context.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and conceptual framework for 'downstream' default effects, synthesizing when defaults' immediate effects persist, fade, or reverse across subsequent consumer decisions.
methodology: Conceptual review and theoretical framework paper synthesizing the consumer default-effect literature. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a general model for predicting whether our round-up default's initial enrollment lift will persist or decay, and what factors moderate that — directly informs how we should measure success beyond signup, not just enrollment rate.
limitations: theoretical/conceptual, not a new empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
abstract gives no effect sizes
relevance_reason: General consumer-behavior framework for downstream default persistence, matching the brief's core question of whether the enrollment lift lasts at 6-12 months.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization, and beneficiary passivity is highly insensitive even to substantial losses from staying with a bad default, with active-choice variation driven by transitory shocks rather than attentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default options among low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Shows default persistence can be extremely strong and largely insensitive to outcome value — a caution against assuming our round-up default's effect will fade the way the retirement literature suggests, and a warning that passivity can mask real harm for those defaulted badly.
limitations: health insurance/drug benefit setting, not consumer savings
government administrative program, not a self-directed app
no financial contribution-amount analogy
relevance_reason: Strong, persistent default-effect evidence with a distributional focus on low-income beneficiaries, relevant to the brief's concern about who is helped or hurt by defaults, despite the different domain.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics undermine the measured effect of automatic enrollment and default auto-escalation: steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from auto-enrollment and 0.3% from auto-escalation, and only 40% of employees escalate on their first scheduled date.
methodology: Analysis of nine 401(k) plans accounting for job separation, withdrawal at separation, and auto-escalation opt-out.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantified statement of our support team's objection: the enrollment lift is real at signup but its effect on actual saving shrinks dramatically over time — directly bearing on whether opt-out enrollment is a vanity metric.
limitations: retirement 401(k) plans rather than liquid consumer savings
employer-mediated setting
relevance_reason: Contradicts the premise that defaults reliably raise saving long-term, exactly the persistence evidence the brief asked for.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment of low-income employees into the public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, though most individuals actively opted out, with the default effect strongest when incentives are high and enrollment-status knowledge is low.
methodology: Administrative and survey data analysis of a nationwide public pension auto-enrollment policy.
why_it_matters: Quantifies a default effect size (23pp) in a low-stakes, simple-choice context and shows the effect is weaker when incentives are low and opting out is easy — relevant to predicting how big our opt-out lift will be for a low-stakes round-up feature.
limitations: public pay-as-you-go pension system, not consumer fintech
government administrative default, not a self-directed app
relevance_reason: Provides an effect size for opt-out default enrollment and shows moderation by incentive size and choice complexity, informing expectations for a low-stakes consumer feature.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's participation and contribution gains attenuate substantially between 12 and 36 months, though it still reduces inequality in savings; a life-cycle model estimates the effective switching cost at about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the persistence question the brief asks about — default gains shrink over medium-run horizons — while showing defaults reduce inequality in savings, a distributional benefit to weigh against disengagement costs.
limitations: employer/national retirement plans, not a consumer app
36-month horizon still shorter than a full career
not a liquid consumer product
relevance_reason: Best available quantification of default-effect attenuation over time in the closest analogous (retirement) literature, central to the brief's persistence question.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a representative five-country European sample (n=4207), default nudges produced medium-to-large effects on investment risk-taking but also lowered ratings of the wealth manager's advice — especially when the default was refused — with perceived honesty mediating the effect.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European survey experiment (n=4207) on default-framed investment allocation.
why_it_matters: Direct EU evidence that defaults can be perceived as less trustworthy or manipulative when refused, and that presentation framing shifts the level people choose — bears squarely on both the reputational-risk and anchoring questions the brief raises for the round-up entry and level decisions.
limitations: investment risk allocation setting, not round-up savings specifically
one-shot experimental ratings, no field or behavioral persistence data
relevance_reason: EU-based experimental evidence on default effect size, level framing/anchoring, and perceived manipulation — matches nearly every open question in the brief for a consumer financial-advice context.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment raised participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants anchored on the low default savings rate and conservative default fund, with half still at the default after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a preset default level strongly anchors contribution-rate choices — the core precedent behind our concern that a preset round-up multiplier will anchor most users at that level rather than a higher one.
limitations: classic, dated employer 401(k) study with no publication year given
employer-mediated trust relationship does not carry to a consumer app
no comparison to opt-in or active choice
relevance_reason: Foundational anchoring-on-default-level finding that the current literature (and this brief) continues to argue with; directly informs the round-up multiplier preset decision despite the different setting.

key_finding: A structural model decomposing default adherence into deviation cost and opt-out cost, estimated on 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions, finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions, and that adding an intermediate preset option (15%) captures 69% of achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million real tipping transactions plus a stated-preference survey, with counterfactual menu-design simulations.
why_it_matters: Its friction-decomposition method and menu-redesign counterfactual transfer directly to our preset multiplier decision: it shows how adding an intermediate preset level between existing options can capture most of the achievable welfare gain without changing underlying frictions — directly actionable for deciding among 1x/2x/5x and which to pre-select.
limitations: tipping decisions, not financial savings
single deviation-cost/opt-out-cost model may not capture savings-specific psychology
no persistence or withdrawal outcomes measured
relevance_reason: Explicit structural method for how preset menu options anchor choices and how welfare gains from menu redesign are quantified — a direct method transfer to the round-up multiplier preset-level decision despite the differing product.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term liquid savings account offered via payroll deduction at UK firms saw very low take-up (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees), but among those who joined, 96% still held a balance and 87% received a payroll contribution at month 12.
methodology: Field study of opt-in payroll-deduction short-term savings accounts introduced at five UK firms with 12-month administrative follow-up.
why_it_matters: The closest existing analog to our round-up feature (liquid, withdrawable, short-term savings) and shows the classic opt-in problem — near-zero take-up — but strong retention once opted in, informing the opt-in versus opt-out trade-off for our design.
limitations: employer payroll-mediated, not a standalone consumer app
no comparison to opt-out or active-choice enrollment
UK employer sample, not a EU consumer banking app
relevance_reason: A liquid, withdrawable, non-retirement savings product — much closer to our round-up feature than pension studies — quantifying opt-in take-up and post-enrollment persistence.

key_finding: Develops a general theoretical characterization of optimal default options (opt-out minimization versus maximization) under asymptotic conditions, extended to cases with externalities, Pigouvian fees, and normative ambiguity.
methodology: Theoretical/mathematical model verified with numerical simulations. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a general normative framework for when a default should minimize versus maximize opt-out, useful background for the entry-mechanism decision, though it gives no empirical effect sizes or consumer-specific evidence.
limitations: purely theoretical, no empirical setting or population
no application to financial savings or consumer apps
abstract gives no numeric effect sizes
relevance_reason: General economic theory of optimal default design, useful as background for the entry-mechanism decision but not tied to any consumer or financial setting.

key_finding: Maps EU laws on dark patterns and develops a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations to distinguish acceptable choice-architecture influence from manipulative practices, including pre-selected defaults.
methodology: Legal-doctrinal analysis and normative taxonomy construction; abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Directly frames when an opt-out default for the round-up feature would read as a lawful nudge versus a regulated dark pattern under EU law, which should shape how the entry decision and its exit mechanism are designed and disclosed.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not an empirical estimate of enrollment or savings effects
no financial-product-specific case studies given in the abstract
relevance_reason: Gives the EU regulatory yardstick for judging whether the chosen default design (especially opt-out) risks being classified as manipulative.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had opted out by 12 months (versus ~50% opt-out at lower defaults in the literature), but many who stayed at the default were contributing a likely-suboptimal amount, especially lower earners.
methodology: Administrative panel data from a single employer plan with a high default, compared against a literature review of lower-default plans.
why_it_matters: Shows that raising a default's level changes opt-out behavior and strongly anchors people at the preset value even when it is a poor fit for them — directly relevant to choosing which round-up multiplier to pre-select.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app the user chose
no employer-as-intermediary comparison to isolate what carries over to fintech
relevance_reason: Empirically quantifies how a preset default level anchors contribution amounts, bearing on the multiplier pre-selection decision.

key_finding: Reports on four large U.K. field experiments automating short-term (non-retirement) payroll savings, but the abstract text supplied is corrupted and gives no usable findings.
methodology: abstract-only; the supplied abstract text is garbled ('Trant') so design details cannot be assessed beyond the title and author list.
why_it_matters: Short-term, liquid payroll savings automation is the closest known analogue to a round-up feature, so if readable this paper likely bears directly on entry-design choice, but no evidence can currently be extracted from it.
limitations: abstract is missing/corrupted, so no effect sizes, sample, or outcomes can be reported
unclear whether these are consumer-directed or employer-payroll-linked accounts
relevance_reason: Title and authorship (Choi, Beshears, Laibson) suggest close relevance to short-term liquid savings automation, but content cannot be verified from the abstract given.

key_finding: At-scale field experiments automatically enrolling U.K. bank customers into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduced unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, implying £170-240 million in market-wide annual savings, though alerts captured less than half of potential avoidable savings.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments run directly through major U.K. retail banks' own apps/systems.
why_it_matters: Demonstrates that automatic (opt-out-style) enrollment into a bank-app feature works at scale without an employer intermediary, directly supporting the feasibility case for opt-out entry into the round-up feature in the same consumer-banking channel.
limitations: measures a different feature (alerts, not savings enrollment)
no data on retention or amounts saved over 6-12 months
relevance_reason: Same industry and delivery channel as the product being built, showing a consumer-bank automatic-enrollment default working at scale without employer trust as the mechanism.

key_finding: Over 41 months, U.K. pension auto-enrollment raised average pension savings by £32-38/month but this was partially offset by increases of £7/month in unsecured debt, alongside modest increases in mortgage uptake and balances.
methodology: Randomized roll-out of automatic enrollment pensions to ~160,000 small U.K. employers, tracked longitudinally.
why_it_matters: Directly undercuts the 'defaults always help' premise by showing nominal savings gains from a default are partly offset by increased debt elsewhere in the household balance sheet — a caution for claiming round-up savings as unambiguous net benefit.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension, not a self-directed liquid consumer product
debt substitution effects may differ for small round-up amounts versus pension-scale contributions
relevance_reason: Long-run (41-month) evidence that default-driven savings gains can be partially illusory once offsetting debt behavior is accounted for, directly relevant to the 'is enrollment vanity' question.

key_finding: Adding a minor extra enrollment step (an 'ordeal') to a health-insurance auto-enrollment policy reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal/addition of an auto-enrollment step in a public health-insurance program, with a theoretical adverse-selection model.
why_it_matters: Shows concretely how added friction in the entry design (moving away from auto-enrollment toward opt-in-like steps) can produce large, demographically skewed enrollment losses — a direct warning about who gets excluded if the round-up feature is opt-in only.
limitations: health insurance selection market with adverse-selection dynamics not present in a savings product
not a financial savings or banking app setting
relevance_reason: Quantifies large, distributionally skewed enrollment losses from added friction, informing the equity risk of choosing opt-in over opt-out or active choice.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, automatic (passive) employer contributions raised total saving substantially, while tax subsidies requiring active choice mostly just shifted assets between accounts, with each $1 of subsidy raising saving by only 1 cent; ~85% of people are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by defaults.
methodology: Large-scale administrative panel data for the full Danish population, comparing active-choice subsidy policies to passive default-contribution policies.
why_it_matters: The classic large-sample demonstration that passive/default mechanisms move far more people than active-choice incentives, and that responsiveness differs sharply between financially sophisticated 'active' and unsophisticated 'passive' individuals — a distributional pattern the round-up team should expect to see mirrored.
limitations: Danish retirement/tax-advantaged account system, not a consumer banking app
government subsidy policy rather than a private-app choice-architecture decision
relevance_reason: Foundational large-N evidence on the passive/active saver split and the outsized effect of defaults over active-choice incentives, the empirical backbone much later fintech work argues with.

key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' (active choice framed to highlight losses from the non-preferred option) as an alternative to opt-out defaults when automatic enrollment is infeasible or ethically fraught.
methodology: Literature review plus two field experiments testing active-choice and enhanced-active-choice designs against defaults.
why_it_matters: Gives a concrete design pattern for capturing more of the default's enrollment benefit through active choice without full auto-enrollment, directly relevant to evaluating the 'active choice' option for entry into the round-up feature.
limitations: field experiments reported are in medication-adherence/health contexts, not consumer finance
no data on savings amounts or 6-12 month persistence
relevance_reason: Directly compares active choice (and an enhanced variant) against defaults, the core question behind whether active choice can substitute for opt-out.

key_finding: Synthesizes household-finance evidence across savings, borrowing, payments, asset allocation, and insurance, and reviews interventions including choice architecture and product design used to shape financial behavior.
methodology: Narrative review/handbook chapter synthesizing the behavioral household finance literature; abstract gives no pooled effect sizes.
why_it_matters: Provides a broad, current synthesis of which choice-architecture levers (including defaults) reliably move household financial behavior versus which do not, useful as a sanity check against over-relying on a single default-effect study.
limitations: narrative overview, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
covers household finance broadly rather than round-up/micro-savings apps specifically
relevance_reason: The review/synthesis anchor the brief asks for, spanning several of the exact mechanisms (defaults, product design, choice architecture) the two decisions depend on.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85% at three firms, but ~80% of participants initially accepted the low default contribution rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half still did after three years, roughly offsetting the accumulation gains from higher participation.
methodology: Multi-year administrative panel data from three large firms comparing pre- and post-automatic-enrollment cohorts.
why_it_matters: The founding demonstration that a preset default level strongly anchors behavior for years, and that anchoring at a poorly chosen default can cancel out the participation gains from auto-enrollment — exactly the risk in shipping a pre-selected round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer 401(k) plans with employer-selected defaults, not a self-directed consumer app
predates the fintech/mobile and EU dark-pattern regulatory context the brief cares about
relevance_reason: The classic evidence that anchoring at a preset default level can offset the enrollment benefit of a default — directly on point for whether to pre-select a multiplier and which one.

key_finding: Randomly assigning default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account increased participation by 40 percentage points, an effect the authors attribute to present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and it also made people more likely to actively choose to save afterward.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with multiple treatment arms designed to isolate mechanisms behind the default effect.
why_it_matters: Identifies the psychological mechanisms (present bias, cognitive cost) driving default effects independent of employer trust, informing whether a similar mechanism would operate in a self-directed banking-app setting.
limitations: salary-linked account in a developing-economy employment context, not a liquid consumer banking app
does not report outcomes beyond the study period
relevance_reason: Provides mechanistic evidence for why defaults work, useful for judging whether the effect would transfer to a setting without an employer intermediary.

key_finding: In a Brazilian fintech field experiment, payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised checking-account overdraft fees by 9%, concentrated among users with a history of overdraft use, so overdraft-prone users saw a net 5% increase in fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment on a consumer financial-management platform in Brazil.
why_it_matters: Shows directly, in a comparable consumer fintech setting, that a well-intentioned nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — the exact distributional failure mode the brief warns against building unknowingly.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or round-up savings specifically
single-country, single-platform sample
relevance_reason: A consumer fintech RCT demonstrating heterogeneous, sometimes harmful, effects of a nudge, directly supporting the brief's concern about who is helped versus hurt by design defaults.
